title: Who Gets the Shade?
script: Host: [welcoming] Your city has funding for fifty new street trees. Why is choosing locations more complicated than finding empty pavement?
Guest: Because shade is a public benefit, and it is often distributed unevenly. We need temperature data, pedestrian routes, existing tree cover, and input from residents who use the streets.
Host: Would you simply plant in the hottest areas?
Guest: [carefully] Heat matters, but so do underground utilities, road safety, water access, and whether a species can survive there. A dead tree provides no long-term shade.
Host: Some business owners worry that roots or falling leaves will create costs.
Guest: Those concerns should be assessed, not dismissed. Good design includes suitable species, enough soil space, maintenance responsibility, and a process for reporting damage.
Host: [curious] What about neighbourhoods that submit the most requests?
Guest: Request numbers can favour places with more time and digital access. Outreach should include renters, older residents, street vendors, and people who do not attend formal meetings.
Host: Who should decide the final list?
Guest: The authority remains accountable, but the criteria should be public. Residents can see why one street was prioritised and when another will be reviewed.
Host: [reflective] Planting photographs usually receive attention. Maintenance does not.
Guest: Exactly. The budget must cover watering, pruning, replacement, and monitoring—not only the launch event.
Host: How would you measure success?
Guest: Tree survival, canopy growth, surface temperatures, pedestrian comfort, and whether benefits reach areas that previously had little shade. We should publish those results each year.
Guest: Do not promise that trees alone will solve urban heat. They are one part of a wider plan involving buildings, transport, water, and safe public space.
